cases.answer: React re-renders a component when its state changes, when its parent re-renders, or when a context it consumes changes. Props changing is really a consequence of the parent rendering. By default every child re-renders with the parent even if its props are the same. To avoid unnecessary renders I first profile with the React DevTools profiler, because most re-renders are cheap. If something is actually slow I wrap it in React.memo, and then keep props referentially stable with useCallback and useMemo, otherwise memo does nothing. Often the better fix is structural: moving state down closer to where it's used, or splitting a big context so unrelated consumers don't update.

So a component re-renders when its state or props change. To avoid extra renders you can use React.memo and also useMemo and useCallback so functions aren't recreated every render. I used useCallback a lot in my dashboard project.
Um, React uses the virtual DOM, so it compares the old and new virtual DOM and only updates what changed, so it's already pretty fast. I think you can use keys too, uh, to make it faster.
React only re-renders when you call forceUpdate or when the page reloads. Normally you use useEffect to stop re-renders by returning false from it.

First I'd clarify the requirements: limits per API key or per user, and whether we allow short bursts. I'd use a token bucket per key: it allows bursts up to the bucket size but enforces the average rate. Because we run many API servers, the counters have to live in a shared store like Redis, and the check and decrement must be atomic, so I'd do it in a Lua script. When a client is over the limit we return 429 with a Retry-After header. I'd also think about what happens if Redis is down, probably fail open for most endpoints, and use a stricter limit per IP on login to stop brute force.

In my internship, a teammate wanted to rewrite our Express API in a new framework two weeks before a demo. I thought the risk was too high. Instead of arguing opinions, I suggested we list what problems the rewrite would actually solve, and it turned out the main issue was slow response times from one endpoint. I profiled it, found a missing database index, and fixed it in a day. We agreed to revisit the rewrite after the demo, and eventually we didn't need it. What I learned is to turn disagreements into a shared problem statement with data, and I've done that in every design discussion since.
I usually get along with everyone. If there's a disagreement we just discuss it and go with the best idea. Communication is really important in a team.
My teammate kept pushing bad code and wouldn't listen to me, so I just rewrote his parts myself at night. The project got done, but he wasn't happy. I still think I was right.

I chose MongoDB because an interview is naturally one document: the plan, the turns, and the evaluations are nested and always read together, and the evaluation shape was changing a lot while I iterated on prompts. The trade-off is weaker relational queries, but I don't need joins much. At a million users, the first thing I'd fix is document growth: I used to store base64 audio inside the interview document, which is terrible, so I'd move audio to object storage. Then I'd add compound indexes on userId and createdAt for the history page, and eventually shard by userId since all queries are per user.
MongoDB is NoSQL so it's more scalable than SQL, and it's easy to use with Node. For a million users I would just scale it up, maybe use a bigger cluster on Atlas.

For scaling, yeah, maybe caching with Redis could help too.

First I'd rule out a data problem: check whether event logging or the pipeline broke, for example compare with server-side logs and see if the drop is in one event type only. If the data is real, I'd segment the drop with SQL by platform, app version, country and acquisition channel. If it's concentrated in, say, Android on the latest version, it's probably a release bug, so I'd check the crash rate and funnel conversion at each step. If it's across all segments, I'd look at external causes like a holiday, an outage or a competitor launch. Then I'd report the likely cause, the evidence, and the size of the impact.
I would look at the dashboard to see when it started dropping and check with the engineering team if there was a release. Maybe also compare with last week's numbers.

A process has its own memory space, so processes are isolated and communicate through pipes, queues or sockets. Threads live inside one process and share its memory, which makes communication cheap but needs locks to avoid race conditions. In CPython the GIL means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so threads don't speed up CPU-bound work. I'd use threads or asyncio for I/O-bound work like many HTTP calls, and multiprocessing, for example a ProcessPoolExecutor, for CPU-bound work like image processing.
A process is a running program and a thread is a smaller unit inside a process. Threads share memory. In Python there's the GIL so threads can be slow.
Threads are just faster processes. In Python you should always use threads because they run on multiple cores at the same time, and processes are old and deprecated.
